title: Computational Complexity of Constructibility (OQ-03)
description: Formalizes the computational complexity of determining whether an algebraic number is constructible by compass and straightedge. Proves power-of-2 testing, the degree criterion hierarchy, the Galois check refinement, and small-degree decidability.

overview.historicalContext: Pierre Wantzel (1837) first proved that angle trisection and cube doubling are impossible with compass and straightedge. His proof relies on showing that constructible numbers have minimal polynomial degree equal to a power of 2. The full characterization via Galois groups (OQ-02) was developed through the work of Galois and later algebraists. OQ-03 asks about the computational side: how efficiently can we determine constructibility? The degree check is fast (polynomial time), but the Galois group computation can be exponential in the worst case.
overview.problemStatement:
OQ-03: What is the computational complexity of determining whether an algebraic number (given by its minimal polynomial) is constructible?

The decision procedure has two levels:
1. Degree check (necessary, O(log d)): Is the degree a power of 2?
2. Galois group check (sufficient, up to O(d!)): Is Gal(f/Q) a 2-group?
overview.text: Formalizes the computational complexity of determining whether an algebraic number is constructible by compass and straightedge. Proves power-of-2 testing, the degree criterion hierarchy, the Galois check refinement, and small-degree decidability.
overview.proofStrategy:
1. Define IsPowerOfTwo and prove basic properties
2. Show key non-examples: 3, 6 are not powers of 2
3. Prove the refinement: Galois check implies degree check
4. Classify small degrees 1-4 completely
5. State the complexity hierarchy
keyInsights: The degree check (power of 2?) is a fast O(log d) necessary condition
The Galois group computation is the bottleneck, up to O(d!) worst case
For degrees 1-2, the degree check is also sufficient (always constructible)
For degree 3, the degree check rules out constructibility immediately
For degree 4+, the Galois group structure matters beyond just the degree

sections.title: Power of 2 Testing
sections.summary: Defines IsPowerOfTwo and proves: 1 is a power of 2, powers of 2 close under doubling, 3 and 6 are not powers of 2.
sections.mathContext: Power-of-2 testing is the first step in the constructibility decision procedure.

sections.title: Degree Criterion
sections.summary: Formalizes the necessary condition: constructible implies degree is a power of 2.
sections.mathContext: The degree check is O(1) given the minimal polynomial and catches all degree-3 obstructions.

sections.title: Decision Hierarchy
sections.summary: Defines the two-level decision hierarchy: degree check (fast, necessary) and Galois check (slow, sufficient). Proves the refinement.
sections.mathContext: Galois check implies degree check via: divisor of $2^k$ is $2^j$.

sections.title: Complexity Classification
sections.summary: Small-degree decidability (degrees 1-4 classified) and complexity summary.
sections.mathContext: For degrees $\leq 2$: always constructible. Degree 3: never. Degree 4+: Galois check needed.

conclusion.summary: The constructibility decision problem has a natural two-level structure: a fast degree check (necessary) and a slower Galois group computation (sufficient). For practical purposes, the degree check eliminates most non-constructible cases immediately.
conclusion.implications: The exponential worst-case complexity of Galois group computation means that for high-degree polynomials, constructibility may be hard to determine. However, for specific polynomial families (cyclotomic, radical extensions), much faster algorithms exist.
openQuestions: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for constructibility that avoids full Galois group computation?
Can the Galois group of specific families be computed in polynomial time?
What is the average-case complexity over random polynomials?
